Methods

Source: vignettes/methods.Rmd
methods.Rmd

Setup

Take a simulation whose outcome at time t depends on n factors, Y_t = f_t(x_1, \ldots, x_n). Each factor has an observed trajectory x_i^1, the one the calibrated model uses, and a counterfactual trajectory x_i^0. The goal is to split the total difference

\Delta Y_t = f_t(x_1^1, \ldots, x_n^1) - f_t(x_1^0, \ldots, x_n^0)

into contributions \delta_i with \sum_i \delta_i = \Delta Y_t exactly.

Factorial design

For n factors there are 2^n on/off combinations. make_run_table() enumerates them, and shapley_decompose() runs the model once per row.

make_run_table(c("a", "b", "c"))
#>    run_id     a     b     c
#>     <int> <int> <int> <int>
#> 1:      1     0     0     0
#> 2:      2     1     0     0
#> 3:      3     0     1     0
#> 4:      4     1     1     0
#> 5:      5     0     0     1
#> 6:      6     1     0     1
#> 7:      7     0     1     1
#> 8:      8     1     1     1

Shapley values

Following Shapley (1953), treat the set S of factors held at their observed values as a coalition, with value v(S) = f_t(x_S^1, x_{N \setminus S}^0). The Shapley value of factor i is its marginal effect averaged over every coalition of the other factors:

\phi_i = \sum_{S \subseteq N \setminus \{i\}} \frac{|S|!\,(n - |S| - 1)!}{n!}\,\bigl[v(S \cup \{i\}) - v(S)\bigr].

It is the only allocation that is efficient (the shares sum to \Delta Y_t), symmetric (interchangeable factors get equal shares), additive, and gives zero to a factor that never changes the outcome.

Interactions are split evenly. In the example below, the outcome is 10 + 5a + 3b + 2ab. Factor a gets its main effect plus half of the interaction, and factor b gets the same treatment:

rt <- make_run_table(c("a", "b"))
rt[, y := 10 + 5 * a + 3 * b + 2 * a * b]
decomp_algebra(rt, list(summary_vars = "y", decomp_vars = c("a", "b"),
                        decomp_method = "shapley"))
#>    measure     a     b
#>     <char> <num> <num>
#> 1:       y     6     4

Das Gupta’s standardization is the same thing

Das Gupta’s (1993) symmetric standardization, the classical demographic tool, weights each marginal effect by 1 / \bigl[n \binom{n-1}{k}\bigr], where k = |S|. Expanding the binomial gives

\frac{1}{n \binom{n-1}{k}} = \frac{k!\,(n-1-k)!}{n \cdot (n-1)!} = \frac{k!\,(n-k-1)!}{n!},

which is the Shapley weight. For binary factors the two methods are identical, so the package implements one weight formula. method = "das_gupta" is accepted as a deprecated alias for "shapley".

Counterfactual types

What x_i^0 is determines the question being answered.

cf_type x_i^0(t) Question
"total_impact" 0 (no programme) How much did this factor avert, in total?
"change_since" x_i(t_0), held at baseline_year How much of the change since t_0 is due to this factor?

Your get_baseline_value() and build_counterfactual() methods implement these definitions for your model’s parameters. For example, “zero” for a coverage factor might mean no coverage, while for a rate it might mean a reference rate.

Counterfactuals in between on and off

Every factor is either observed or counterfactual, but the counterfactual does not have to be zero. To ask what coverage above some reference achieved, such as half of observed coverage or a target level, define that reference as the counterfactual in your model’s get_baseline_value() and build_counterfactual(). The decomposition is unchanged and still needs 2^n runs per step. It attributes the difference between the observed world and the reference world.

Two related questions are different methods, not settings of this one. Splitting credit along a continuous path from off to observed is the Aumann-Shapley value, which differs from the Shapley value only when factors interact non-linearly. Asking what would happen at 50% coverage is a scenario projection, not an attribution.

Decomposing over time: sequential Shapley

Simulations carry state forward. Infections averted in 2005 change the susceptible pool in 2010. A single decomposition at a late year would credit every past policy at once, so shapley_decompose() works year by year, using the sequential Shapley construction of Carter (2025).

At each decomposition year y:

  • every policy before y is at its observed value;
  • every policy after y is at its counterfactual;
  • only the year-y policy varies across the 2^n coalitions.

The Shapley value at step y is therefore the marginal impact of the year-y policy, conditional on the past and undiluted by the future. Because the model is simulated forward from y, extended_decomp records that step’s effect at every later year T \ge y, written \phi_i^{(y)}(T). sequential_totals() sums the steps:

\text{total}_i(T) = \sum_{y \le T} \phi_i^{(y)}(T).

Summed over factors, this telescopes to observed minus all-off from the first decomposition year at every T, so the totals stay exact. That only holds when decomp_years is contiguous, and sequential_totals() checks it.

Runs that are not simulated

Exact Shapley values need all 2^n coalitions at every step, but two kinds of coalition repeat a run that already exists:

  • the coalition with every factor off at step y (counterfactual from y) is the same scenario as the coalition with every factor on at step y-1;
  • a factor whose counterfactual leaves the step’s parameters unchanged, such as a programme that has not started yet, is a null player. Switching it on or off gives the same run, so its Shapley value at that step is 0.

shapley_decompose() simulates each distinct scenario once. It confirms that the parameters are identical before reusing a run, so a reused run always equals the one it replaces. run_summary in the result reports, for each step, how many runs were simulated and which factors were null.

References

Shapley LS (1953). A value for n-person games. In Kuhn HW, Tucker AW (eds), Contributions to the Theory of Games II, 307–317. Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400881970-018

Das Gupta P (1993). Standardization and Decomposition of Rates: A User’s Manual. Current Population Reports P23-186. U.S. Bureau of the Census. https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/1993/demographics/p23-186.pdf

Carter A (2025). Quantifying averted burden from infectious disease control policies. PhD dissertation, University of Washington. https://hdl.handle.net/1773/53310

Carter A. A model-agnostic framework for factorial decomposition of discrete-time simulation outcomes, with a proof of equivalence between Das Gupta and Shapley value decomposition. Manuscript in preparation.
